summary: This program asks the builder for a house's address, bedroom and bathroom counts, and then for each room in the layout its use and dimensions. It stores the answers in House and Room objects and prints a summary of the finished plan.

lines.text: ArrayList is the resizable list implementation used to collect the rooms as they are entered.
A single Scanner reads every answer the builder types at the keyboard.
nextLine reads the whole line, so an address with spaces in it stays intact.
Bathrooms are a decimal because half baths are common in real listings.
Knowing the number of rooms up front tells the loop below how many times to repeat.
nextInt leaves the newline behind, so this extra nextLine throws it away before the loop reads a room's use as text.
The list is declared as List but created as an ArrayList, a habit that lets you swap the implementation later without touching this code.
Counting from 1 up to roomCount collects one set of answers per room and gives the prompts human-friendly numbers.
The three answers are bundled into one Room object, which keeps a room's use and size together instead of in three loose variables.

lines.code: House house = new House(address, bedrooms, bathrooms);
lines.text: The constructor sets the house's basic facts at the moment it is created.
The layout is attached afterwards with a setter because the rooms were not known until the loop finished.
Moving the display work into its own method keeps main focused on gathering input.
This helper is private because only HouseBuilder needs it, and static because it belongs to the class rather than to any object.
size() reports how many rooms the list actually holds, which double-checks the count that was typed in.
The enhanced for loop visits each Room in turn without you having to manage an index.
Each room reports its own details through its getters, which is the whole point of storing them as objects.
